title: How Amarone Evolves with Age
quiz.0.question: How much weight do the grapes lose during appassimento?
quiz.0.explanation: During appassimento the grapes usually lose 30-40% of their weight in water, concentrating sugar, acidity, polyphenols and aroma precursors.
quiz.1.question: When does Amarone's first drinking peak (0-10 years) usually occur?
quiz.1.options.0: 0-3 years, when the fruit is freshest
quiz.1.options.2: 8-10 years, when the tannins start to soften
quiz.1.explanation: Amarone's first drinking window is usually at 4-7 years, when the rich fruit and oak begin to integrate; the tannins are still firm, but the wine is already enjoyable.
quiz.2.question: Which producer style description correctly matches "modern Amarone"?
quiz.2.options.0: Large old Slavonian casks, high acidity, floral
quiz.2.options.1: New French oak, earlier pressing off the skins, rich dark fruit, round and modern
quiz.2.options.2: No oak ageing, focused on preserving raw fruit
quiz.2.explanation: Modern Amarone producers (such as Allegrini) favour small new French oak barrels that add vanilla and mocha, and press off the skins earlier to keep the fruit fresh, giving a round, easy style with a relatively early drinking window.
quiz.3.question: What is the deadliest mistake when storing Amarone?
quiz.3.explanation: Temperature fluctuation is the greatest enemy of ageing: expansion and contraction make the cork repeatedly shrink and swell, letting oxygen in; a stable cool temperature (12-14°C), even slightly below ideal, is far better than an unstable environment.

slides.2.title: The Appassimento Process: The Science
slides.2.content:
The Science of Drying: The Magic of Concentration

Water loss: grapes are dried for 90-120 days, losing 30-40% of their weight, concentrating sugar, acidity, polyphenols and aroma precursors
The role of botrytis: a moderate amount of noble rot (Botrytis cinerea) adds complex honey and nut notes, but too much infection lowers quality
The key: 8-12°C + 65-75% relative humidity + good ventilation — all three are essential

The Wine After Drying

📊 Alcohol: 15-17% ABV (compared with 12% for ordinary Valpolicella)
🍇 Residual sugar: usually under 12 g/L (almost fully dry); sweet Recioto keeps 80-200 g/L
🔬 Concentrated polyphenols: anthocyanins and tannins clearly higher than in ordinary Valpolicella, the basis of very long ageing potential
slides.3.title: Evolution at 0-10 Years: Three Drinking Windows
slides.3.content:
0-3 years

Closed phase

Just bottled, dominated by oak, with grippy tannins and suppressed fruit — not recommended for drinking. Needs at least 3-4 hours of decanting in advance, or more time in the cellar.

4-7 years

First drinking window

The fruit (blackberry, prune, chocolate) begins to integrate and the oak blends in; tannins are still firm but already silky. For lovers of a powerful young style; decant for 2 hours.

8-10 years

Entering development

Tannins begin to soften, and the dried-fruit aromas move towards secondary notes of leather, tobacco and spice as aged complexity first appears — the starting point favoured by traditionalists.
slides.4.title: Evolution at 11-30 Years and the Legendary Realm
slides.4.content:
🍫 11-15 years: maturity

Preparing for the peak

Leather, cinnamon, black truffle; silky tannins; fruit moving to dried fig and date; harmonious and elegant overall

🌹 16-20 years: the first peak

The traditionalist's favourite drinking period

Aromas fully open: flowers + leather + spice + aged complexity; fresh acidity in support; tannins absorbed into the body; the best point of balance

🏆 21-30 years: the legendary realm

Top vintages + top producers

Agarwood, cigar box, aged rose, truffle; only perfectly stored top wines reach this realm; Quintarelli is the benchmark

📉 30+ years: decline

Only the greatest vintages survive

Ordinary wines begin to lose vitality; fruit fades; top wines such as Quintarelli and Dal Forno Romano remain captivating
slides.5.title: Top Producer Styles Compared
slides.5.content:
Traditional (Quintarelli)

  • Large old Slavonian oak casks
  • Very long cask ageing (about 7 years before bottling)
  • High acidity, high tannin, powerful structure
  • Ageing potential: 25-40 years
  • Drinking window: after 12-25 years

Modern (e.g. Allegrini)

  • Small new French oak barrels (225-500 L)
  • Shorter maceration
  • Round fruit, vanilla and mocha aromas
  • Ageing potential: 15-25 years
  • Drinking window: after 5-15 years

⚖️ In a Class of Its Own: Dal Forno Romano

Based in Val d'Illasi outside the Classico zone, with tiny yields and ageing in new small French oak barrels, extremely concentrated, ageing potential 20-35 years, regarded as a quality benchmark

slides.8.title: Key Takeaways
slides.8.points.0: Appassimento dries grapes for 90-120 days; they lose 30-40% of their water, concentrating sugar, acidity and polyphenols
slides.8.points.1: Ideal drying conditions: 8-12°C, 65-75% humidity, good ventilation — all three are essential
slides.8.points.2: Amarone's first drinking window: 4-7 years; traditionalists prefer to start at 8-10 years
slides.8.points.3: 16-20 years is the first peak of traditional Amarone: aromas fully open, acidity in support, tannins absorbed
slides.8.points.4: Traditional (Quintarelli): large old casks, very long cask ageing, ageing potential 25-40 years
slides.8.points.5: Modern (e.g. Allegrini): new French barrels, round fruit, ageing potential 15-25 years, relatively early maturing and easy to drink
slides.8.points.6: The deadliest storage mistake: temperature fluctuation — a stable cool temperature (12-14°C) matters far more than an unstable environment
slides.8.points.7: Top benchmarks: Quintarelli (traditional) and Dal Forno Romano (extreme concentration) can both age 30+ years
slides.8.points.8: Buying strategy: modern styles suit drinking within 10 years; traditional styles suit long cellaring
